formation_enthalpy.description: This formula defines the standard enthalpy of formation of a compound as the difference between the enthalpy of the compound and the sum of the enthalpies of its constituent elements in their standard states, weighted by stoichiometric coefficients. It quantifies the energy change when one mole of compound is formed from its elements under standard conditions. The enthalpy of elements in their standard states is conventionally taken as zero, simplifying the calculation. This quantity is fundamental in thermochemistry for calculating reaction enthalpies via Hess's law.
formation_enthalpy.history: The concept of formation enthalpy was developed in the 19th century, with key contributions from Marcellin Berthelot and Julius Thomsen who measured heats of reaction. The modern standard-state convention was formalized in the early 20th century by thermochemists like G.N. Lewis and Merle Randall.
formation_enthalpy.applicability: This definition applies to compounds at standard conditions (typically 298 K and 1 bar) and assumes the elements are in their most stable allotropic forms. It breaks down for compounds that cannot be formed directly from elements, where indirect methods must be used. The formula assumes ideal behavior and does not account for temperature or pressure variations unless explicitly included in the enthalpy values.

operators.m: Proportional to

pbh_mass_scale_relation.description: This relation states that the mass of a primordial black hole formed from the collapse of density perturbations is inversely proportional to the square of the perturbation wavenumber. It arises from the causal horizon mass at the time of re-entry of a perturbation mode during the radiation-dominated era. Smaller-scale perturbations (larger k_p) collapse earlier when the horizon mass is smaller, producing lighter black holes. The relation is derived from the Friedmann equation and the scaling of the horizon mass with scale factor.
pbh_mass_scale_relation.history: This scaling was established in the 1970s through the pioneering work of Stephen Hawking and Bernard Carr on primordial black hole formation. The relation was refined in subsequent decades with more detailed collapse calculations.
pbh_mass_scale_relation.applicability: This relation applies to primordial black holes formed in the early universe during radiation domination, assuming spherical collapse and a Gaussian spectrum of perturbations. It breaks down for black holes formed during matter domination or from non-Gaussian perturbations, where the mass scaling differs. The relation also assumes no significant accretion after formation, which may not hold for very massive PBHs.

frequency_scaling_relation.description: This relation states that a high frequency is proportional to the square of a low frequency. It is a scaling law, often encountered in systems with nonlinear dispersion relations or in certain astrophysical contexts. The proportionality constant is not specified, so the relation captures only the functional dependence.
frequency_scaling_relation.applicability: This relation is highly context-dependent and lacks universal validity. It applies only to specific systems where such a quadratic scaling has been derived or observed, such as in certain plasma or condensed-matter phenomena. It breaks down in linear systems or where other power laws hold.

variables.m: Angular diameter distance from lens to source
Angular diameter distance from observer to lens
Angular diameter distance from observer to source

operators.m: Takes the square root of the argument

constants.m: Universal constant of gravitation
Speed of light in vacuum

einstein_ring_angle.description: This formula gives the angular radius of the Einstein ring, a characteristic feature of gravitational lensing in the strong-field regime. It arises from the deflection of light by a point mass in the weak-field approximation of general relativity. The angle depends on the square root of the mass and on the ratio of angular diameter distances. It is derived from the Schwarzschild metric and the geodesic equation for photons.
einstein_ring_angle.history: The concept was first discussed by Einstein in 1936, following earlier work by others on gravitational lensing. The formula in its modern form was developed within the framework of general relativity.
einstein_ring_angle.applicability: This formula applies to a point mass lens in the weak-field, small-angle approximation, assuming a static, spherically symmetric mass distribution. It breaks down for extended mass distributions, strong fields near black holes, or when the thin-lens approximation fails. It also assumes the observer, lens, and source are collinear.

operators.m: Exponential decay with inverse temperature

constants.m: Frequency factor, related to collision frequency and steric effects
Relates temperature to energy

arrhenius_law.description: The Arrhenius law describes the temperature dependence of reaction rates. It states that the rate increases exponentially with decreasing activation energy and increasing temperature. The pre-exponential factor A accounts for the frequency of molecular collisions and the probability of proper orientation. The exponential term represents the fraction of molecules with energy exceeding the activation barrier.
arrhenius_law.history: The law was proposed by Svante Arrhenius in 1889, based on the work of van't Hoff. It was later given a theoretical foundation through collision theory and transition state theory.
arrhenius_law.applicability: This law applies to thermally activated processes, such as chemical reactions and diffusion, in the high-temperature limit where quantum tunneling is negligible. It breaks down at very low temperatures, for reactions involving quantum tunneling, or when the pre-exponential factor itself depends strongly on temperature. It also assumes a single activation energy and a well-defined reaction coordinate.

operators.m: Natural logarithm

constants.m: Relates energy to temperature at the particle level

entropy_formula.description: The Boltzmann entropy formula states that the entropy S of a macroscopic system is proportional to the natural logarithm of the number W of microscopic configurations consistent with its macroscopic state. It provides a statistical definition of entropy, linking thermodynamics to statistical mechanics. The formula holds for isolated systems in equilibrium, where each microstate is equally probable. It is fundamental in understanding the second law of thermodynamics as a tendency toward higher probability.
entropy_formula.history: Formulated by Ludwig Boltzmann in the 1870s, building on the work of James Clerk Maxwell. The modern form with the constant k_B was later popularized by Max Planck.
entropy_formula.applicability: Applies to equilibrium systems with a well-defined number of microstates, typically in the thermodynamic limit. It breaks down for non-equilibrium systems, small systems where fluctuations are significant, and quantum systems where microstates are not equally probable without further assumptions.

operators.m: Combines reactants or products
Indicates direction of transformation

chemical_reaction.description: A chemical reaction equation represents the transformation of reactants (A and B) into products (C and D). It is a symbolic statement of the stoichiometry, showing the relative amounts of each species consumed and produced. The equation must be balanced to conserve mass and charge. It does not imply the reaction goes to completion; it only describes the net change.
chemical_reaction.history: Chemical equations evolved from early alchemical notation in the 17th century to the modern arrow notation introduced by Jean Beguin in 1615 and refined by later chemists like Antoine Lavoisier in the 18th century.
chemical_reaction.applicability: Applies to all chemical reactions under any conditions, but the equation itself does not specify kinetics or equilibrium. It breaks down if the reaction involves multiple steps or intermediates, or if the stoichiometry is not fixed (e.g., non-stoichiometric compounds).

variables.m: Molecule composed of atoms A and B

operators.m: Combines photon with molecule
Indicates transformation

constants.m: Relates photon energy to frequency
Frequency of the incident photon

photodissociation.description: Photodissociation is a process where a molecule AB absorbs a photon of energy hν, leading to its breakup into constituent atoms A and B. The photon's energy must exceed the bond dissociation energy for the reaction to occur. This equation represents a single-step photochemical process, often the first step in atmospheric and interstellar chemistry. It conserves energy, with the photon's energy going into breaking the bond and imparting kinetic energy to the fragments.
photodissociation.history: The concept of photodissociation was established in the early 20th century, with key contributions from Albert Einstein's 1905 explanation of the photoelectric effect and later studies by James Franck and Edward Condon in the 1920s on molecular spectra.
photodissociation.applicability: Applies to gas-phase molecules absorbing photons in the ultraviolet or visible range, where the photon energy matches the bond energy. It breaks down for condensed phases where solvent effects alter dissociation dynamics, for multiphoton processes, or when the molecule has internal relaxation pathways competing with dissociation.

operators.m: Integration over time

continuous_wavelet_transform.description: The continuous wavelet transform (CWT) computes the inner product of a signal x(t) with a family of wavelet functions ψ*_{s,τ}(t), which are scaled and shifted versions of a mother wavelet. The result W(s,τ) measures the similarity between the signal and the wavelet at each scale s and position τ. This provides a time-frequency representation with variable resolution: good frequency resolution at low frequencies and good time resolution at high frequencies. The transform is invertible when the mother wavelet satisfies the admissibility condition.
continuous_wavelet_transform.history: The continuous wavelet transform was developed in the 1980s, building on earlier work by Jean Morlet and Alex Grossmann, who formalized the theory in 1984. It was later connected to earlier ideas in harmonic analysis and group theory.
continuous_wavelet_transform.applicability: The CWT applies to finite-energy signals and requires the mother wavelet to satisfy the admissibility condition for inversion. It breaks down for signals with infinite energy or when the wavelet does not meet the admissibility condition. The transform is not discrete and requires continuous integration, making it computationally intensive for practical applications.

operators.m: Hilbert transform, shifts phase by -90°
Imaginary unit, √(-1)

analytic_signal.description: The analytic signal z(t) is constructed from a real signal x(t) by adding its Hilbert transform as the imaginary part. This creates a complex signal whose real part is the original signal and whose imaginary part is the Hilbert transform. The analytic signal can be expressed in polar form with instantaneous amplitude a(t) and instantaneous phase φ(t). This representation is unique and provides a well-defined way to extract instantaneous frequency and amplitude from a real signal.
analytic_signal.history: The concept of the analytic signal was introduced by Dennis Gabor in 1946 in the context of communication theory. It was later formalized mathematically by Ville in 1948.
analytic_signal.applicability: The analytic signal is applicable to narrowband signals where the concept of instantaneous frequency is meaningful. It breaks down for broadband signals or signals with multiple frequency components, where the instantaneous amplitude and phase become ambiguous. The Hilbert transform requires the signal to be square-integrable and is well-defined for L² functions.

berezinskii_kosterlitz_thouless_transiti.description: The Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition temperature is given by T_BKT = (π/2) ρ_s(0), where ρ_s(0) is the superfluid density at zero temperature (in units where ħ = k_B = 1). This formula describes the temperature at which bound vortex-antivortex pairs unbind in a two-dimensional superfluid. Below this temperature, vortices are bound in pairs and the system exhibits quasi-long-range order. Above T_BKT, free vortices proliferate and destroy superfluidity.
berezinskii_kosterlitz_thouless_transiti.history: The BKT transition was independently predicted by Vadim Berezinskii in 1971 and by John Kosterlitz and David Thouless in 1973. The universal relation T_BKT = (π/2) ρ_s(0) was derived by Nelson and Kosterlitz in 1977.
berezinskii_kosterlitz_thouless_transiti.applicability: This formula applies to two-dimensional superfluids and superconductors with continuous symmetry. It assumes the system is in the thermodynamic limit and that the superfluid density is uniform. The formula breaks down in three dimensions, where true long-range order exists, and in systems with discrete symmetry, where the transition is of a different type. It also assumes the absence of long-range interactions and disorder.

bcs_gap_equation_critical_temperature.description: This equation is the critical condition for the BCS (Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer) pairing instability. It states that when the product of the effective attractive interaction U and the pair susceptibility χ(ω) reaches unity, the normal state becomes unstable against the formation of Cooper pairs. The susceptibility χ(ω) sums over all particle-particle bubble diagrams, and the condition 1 = Uχ(ω) signals a pole in the two-particle Green's function at zero center-of-mass momentum and frequency ω. This marks the onset of superconductivity or superfluidity at the mean-field level.
bcs_gap_equation_critical_temperature.history: This condition was derived by Bardeen, Cooper, and Schrieffer in their 1957 theory of superconductivity. The modern form using the susceptibility and the eigenvalue condition was developed in the context of Eliashberg theory and functional integral approaches in the 1960s.
bcs_gap_equation_critical_temperature.applicability: This condition applies to weakly coupled fermionic systems with a retarded or instantaneous attractive interaction, in the mean-field (BCS) approximation. It breaks down for strong coupling, where the self-consistent gap equation must be solved beyond the simple eigenvalue condition, and for non-equilibrium or inhomogeneous systems where the uniform susceptibility is not sufficient.

thermal_mass_correction.description: This formula gives the leading temperature correction to the effective mass in thermal quantum field theory. At finite temperature, the self-energy of a particle acquires a temperature-dependent contribution, which modifies the pole of the propagator. For a scalar field with quartic interactions, the thermal mass squared increases linearly with T², with the coefficient c determined by the coupling strength and the number of degrees of freedom. This result arises from the leading-order (one-loop) contribution to the self-energy in the imaginary-time formalism.
thermal_mass_correction.history: This result was derived in the 1970s and 1980s in the development of thermal field theory, particularly by Dolan and Jackiw (1974) and Weinberg (1974) for the effective potential at finite temperature. The specific form m² = m₀² + cT² is a standard result for the thermal mass of scalar fields.
thermal_mass_correction.applicability: This formula applies to weakly coupled quantum field theories at high temperature (T >> m₀) and in thermal equilibrium, within the one-loop approximation. It breaks down for strong coupling, near phase transitions where higher-order terms become important, and for fermionic fields where the thermal mass correction has a different functional form (often proportional to T² but with different coefficients and sign).

beer_lambert_law.description: The Beer-Lambert law describes the attenuation of light (or other electromagnetic radiation) as it passes through a homogeneous absorbing medium. The intensity decreases exponentially with the product of the absorption cross-section σ, the number density of absorbers n, and the path length x. This law arises from the differential equation dI/dx = -σnI, which states that the fractional decrease in intensity per unit length is proportional to the density of absorbers and their cross-section. It is fundamental to spectroscopy, atmospheric physics, and optical measurements.
beer_lambert_law.history: The law was independently formulated by Pierre Bouguer in 1729, Johann Heinrich Lambert in 1760, and August Beer in 1852. Beer's contribution was recognizing the dependence on concentration, leading to the modern form used in chemical analysis.
beer_lambert_law.applicability: This law applies to non-scattering, homogeneous media with independent absorbers and monochromatic radiation. It breaks down when scattering is significant, when absorbers interact (high concentrations), when the radiation is not monochromatic, or when the intensity is high enough to cause saturation or multi-photon effects. It also fails for inhomogeneous media where the density varies along the path.

variables.m: Moment of inertia about the axis
Perpendicular distance from the axis to mass element

operators.m: Integration over the entire body

moment_of_inertia.description: The moment of inertia quantifies how mass is distributed relative to a given rotation axis. It is the rotational analogue of mass, appearing in the rotational kinetic energy and angular momentum relations. The integral sums the product of each mass element and the square of its distance from the axis, weighting distant mass more heavily. This definition holds for any rigid body, continuous or discrete, about any axis.
moment_of_inertia.history: The concept was introduced by Leonhard Euler in the 18th century, building on earlier work by Christiaan Huygens. The modern integral formulation was developed in the context of classical mechanics by Euler and later formalized by others.
moment_of_inertia.applicability: This formula applies to rigid bodies in classical mechanics, assuming a fixed axis of rotation. It breaks down for deformable bodies or when relativistic effects become significant. For non-uniform density, the integral must be evaluated with the density function, and for complex geometries numerical methods are often required.

operators.m: Proportional to, up to a constant factor

power_law_cross_section.description: This relation states that the cross section for a scattering or reaction process varies as a power of the incident particle's energy. The exponent α characterizes the energy dependence, which can be positive or negative depending on the interaction. It is often used as a phenomenological fit to experimental data over limited energy ranges. The proportionality constant is not specified here, as it depends on the specific process.
power_law_cross_section.history: Power-law cross sections have been used empirically since the early days of nuclear and particle physics. The specific form arises naturally in many theoretical models, such as the Bethe formula for stopping power or the Rutherford scattering at low energies, but the general power-law form is a common approximation.
power_law_cross_section.applicability: This form applies to processes where the cross section varies smoothly with energy over a limited range. It breaks down near thresholds, resonances, or when multiple channels contribute with different energy dependences. It is not valid at very high energies where relativistic effects or new physics may alter the scaling, nor at very low energies where quantum effects like the Wigner threshold law may dominate.

operators.m: Exponential function
Square root

maxwell_boltzmann_distribution.description: This gives the probability density for the speed of a particle in an ideal gas at thermal equilibrium. The distribution is a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, characterized by the parameter σ, which is related to the temperature and particle mass. The v² factor arises from the volume element in spherical coordinates in velocity space, and the exponential factor comes from the Boltzmann factor. The normalization ensures the total probability integrates to 1.
maxwell_boltzmann_distribution.history: James Clerk Maxwell derived the distribution in 1860, and Ludwig Boltzmann generalized it in the 1870s. The modern form with σ as a scale parameter is a standard representation in statistical mechanics.
maxwell_boltzmann_distribution.applicability: This applies to classical, non-interacting particles in thermal equilibrium, such as a dilute ideal gas. It breaks down for quantum gases (Fermi-Dirac or Bose-Einstein statistics), for strongly interacting systems, or at very low temperatures where quantum effects become important. It also assumes non-relativistic speeds; for relativistic particles, the Maxwell-Jüttner distribution must be used.

stefan_boltzmann_law_cooling.description: This formula describes the cooling of a black body in a regime where the heat capacity is proportional to T^3 (e.g., a degenerate non-relativistic Fermi gas or a photon gas in a fixed volume). It arises from combining the Stefan-Boltzmann law for radiated power (P ∝ T^4) with the energy balance dU/dt = -P, where U ∝ T^4. The solution yields T ∝ τ^{-1/4}, meaning the temperature drops as a power law with exponent -1/4. This is a specific solution valid when the internal energy scales as T^4 and the system loses energy only through surface radiation.
stefan_boltzmann_law_cooling.history: The Stefan-Boltzmann law itself was derived by Josef Stefan (1879) empirically and by Ludwig Boltzmann (1884) theoretically. The specific cooling law T ∝ τ^{-1/4} follows from standard thermodynamic arguments and is often attributed to early 20th-century astrophysical applications, though its exact origin is not uniquely documented.
stefan_boltzmann_law_cooling.applicability: This applies to systems where the internal energy density is proportional to T^4, such as a photon gas in a fixed cavity or a degenerate relativistic Fermi gas. It breaks down when the heat capacity is not ∝ T^3, when the system is not optically thick (so the Stefan-Boltzmann law does not hold), or when other cooling mechanisms (e.g., convection, conduction) dominate. It also assumes a constant volume and no external heat sources.

variables.m: power-law index (positive for decreasing temperature outward)

power_law_temperature_profile.description: This formula expresses a temperature profile that varies as a power of radius, common in astrophysical and geophysical contexts. It is a phenomenological relation often used to model stellar interiors, accretion disks, or planetary atmospheres, where the exponent α depends on the physical processes (e.g., radiative diffusion, convection, or adiabatic gradients). The proportionality constant is set by boundary conditions. It is not a fundamental law but a convenient parametrization that captures the dominant radial dependence.
power_law_temperature_profile.history: Power-law temperature profiles have been used since the early 20th century in stellar structure theory (e.g., in the work of Eddington and later in polytropic models). The specific form T ∝ R^{-α} is a standard assumption in many analytical models, though its origin is not tied to a single discovery.
power_law_temperature_profile.applicability: This applies in regions where the temperature gradient is smooth and can be approximated by a single power law, such as in radiative zones of stars or in thin accretion disks. It breaks down near boundaries, in convective zones where the profile is nearly adiabatic but not a simple power law, or when phase transitions or strong gradients occur. It is also invalid if the exponent α varies significantly with radius.

operators.m: derivative with respect to the natural logarithm of frequency

spectral_index.description: The spectral index β quantifies how the opacity κ depends on frequency ν in a power-law fashion, κ ∝ ν^β. It is defined as the logarithmic derivative of κ with respect to ν, so β is the local slope on a log-log plot. This index is crucial in radiative transfer, determining how radiation of different frequencies interacts with matter. For example, in free-free absorption, β ≈ -3 (for a thermal plasma), while in electron scattering, β = 0.
spectral_index.history: The concept of a spectral index for opacity emerged in the early 20th century with the development of radiative transfer theory, particularly in the works of Schwarzschild, Eddington, and later in the context of stellar atmospheres. The specific definition as a logarithmic derivative is standard in astrophysics.
spectral_index.applicability: This applies to any medium where the opacity can be approximated as a power law in frequency over a limited range. It breaks down when the opacity has a more complex frequency dependence (e.g., with absorption edges or resonances), or when scattering and absorption have different frequency behaviors. It is also invalid if the medium is not in local thermodynamic equilibrium or if the opacity depends on other variables (like temperature or density) in a way that couples with frequency.

variables.m: Magnetic field component along line of sight
Path length along line of sight

operators.m: Integration along the line of sight

constants.m: Charge of a single electron
Rest mass of an electron
Speed of light in vacuum

rotation_measure.description: The rotation measure quantifies the amount of Faraday rotation experienced by linearly polarized electromagnetic radiation as it propagates through a magnetized plasma. It is proportional to the integral of the electron density times the magnetic field component along the line of sight. This formula arises from the difference in phase velocity between left and right circularly polarized waves in a plasma with a magnetic field. The rotation measure is directly observable from the wavelength dependence of the polarization angle.
rotation_measure.history: The effect of Faraday rotation in plasmas was discovered by Michael Faraday in 1845, and the quantitative formula for astrophysical rotation measure was developed in the mid-20th century, notably by Leverett Davis and others in the 1950s.
rotation_measure.applicability: This formula applies to cold, tenuous plasmas where the refractive index is well approximated by the cold plasma dispersion relation. It assumes the magnetic field is slowly varying compared to the wavelength and that the plasma is non-relativistic. It breaks down in dense or relativistic plasmas, where higher-order corrections become significant, and in regions with strong magnetic fields where the cyclotron frequency approaches the wave frequency.

variables.m: Change in velocity of the rocket

operators.m: Natural logarithm of the mass ratio

tsiolkovsky_rocket_equation.description: The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation gives the maximum change in velocity a rocket can achieve by expelling propellant. It states that the delta-v equals the effective exhaust velocity times the natural logarithm of the initial to final mass ratio. This relationship follows from conservation of momentum applied to the rocket and its expelled exhaust. The equation assumes that all propellant is expelled in a direction opposite to the desired motion and that no external forces act on the rocket.
tsiolkovsky_rocket_equation.history: The equation was derived independently by Konstantin Tsiolkovsky in 1903 and later by Robert Goddard and Hermann Oberth in the early 20th century. It is fundamental to rocketry and spaceflight.
tsiolkovsky_rocket_equation.applicability: This equation applies to rockets in vacuum with no external forces (no gravity, no drag) and constant exhaust velocity. It breaks down when external forces are significant, when the exhaust velocity varies during flight, or when relativistic effects become important. It also assumes the propellant is expelled instantaneously in the rocket's rest frame, which is a good approximation for most chemical and electric propulsion systems.

variables.m: Mean molar mass of the gas mixture

constants.m: Universal gas constant relating energy scale to temperature

ideal_gas_law.description: The ideal gas law relates the pressure of a gas to its density, temperature, and mean molar mass. It states that pressure equals density times the gas constant times temperature divided by molar mass. This equation combines Boyle's law, Charles's law, and Avogadro's law into a single relation. It holds for gases where intermolecular interactions are negligible and the volume occupied by the molecules themselves is small compared to the container volume.
ideal_gas_law.history: The ideal gas law was formulated over several centuries, with contributions from Robert Boyle (1662), Jacques Charles (1787), and Amedeo Avogadro (1811). The modern form was established in the 19th century by Émile Clapeyron and others.
ideal_gas_law.applicability: This equation applies to dilute gases at moderate temperatures and pressures, where the gas behaves ideally. It breaks down at high pressures, low temperatures (near condensation), and for gases with strong intermolecular forces. It also fails for relativistic gases or when quantum effects become important, such as in degenerate matter.

operators.m: Sum over all states m except n
Matrix element of perturbation between unperturbed states

perturbation_theory_second_order.description: This formula gives the second-order correction to the energy of a quantum state when a perturbation H' is applied. It sums the squared matrix elements of the perturbation between the state of interest and all other states, divided by the energy difference between those states. The correction is always negative for the ground state, reflecting that perturbations generally lower the ground state energy. This is a cornerstone of quantum mechanical perturbation theory, used when the first-order correction vanishes or is insufficient.
perturbation_theory_second_order.history: Developed by Erwin Schrödinger in 1926 in his foundational papers on perturbation theory, building on earlier work by Lord Rayleigh. The modern form is standard in quantum mechanics textbooks.
perturbation_theory_second_order.applicability: Applies to discrete, non-degenerate spectra where the perturbation is small compared to energy level spacings. Breaks down when energy denominators approach zero (near-degeneracy), requiring degenerate perturbation theory. Also fails for continuous spectra without proper regularization, and for strong perturbations where the series diverges.

pairing_energy.description: This condition states that for a pair of particles to form a bound state, the pairing energy must be negative. A negative pairing energy indicates that the bound state has lower energy than the unbound configuration, making it energetically favorable. This is a fundamental requirement in superconductivity (Cooper pairs) and nuclear physics (pairing correlations). The condition ensures that the interaction between the two particles is attractive enough to overcome kinetic energy costs.
pairing_energy.history: The concept of pairing energy emerged from the BCS theory of superconductivity (Bardeen, Cooper, Schrieffer, 1957) and from nuclear shell model studies in the 1950s. The specific condition U < 0 is a basic thermodynamic requirement for bound state formation.
pairing_energy.applicability: Applies to any two-particle system where pairing is considered, including Cooper pairs in superconductors and nucleon pairs in nuclei. Breaks down when the pairing interaction is momentum-dependent or when many-body effects renormalize the effective pairing energy. Also fails for systems with strong repulsive cores where the simple energy criterion is insufficient.

variables.m: Second derivative of function f at x

operators.m: Approximately equal to

finite_difference_second_derivative.description: This formula approximates the second derivative of a function using values at three equally spaced points. It is derived from the Taylor expansion of f(x+h) and f(x-h) around x, where the first-order terms cancel, leaving the second derivative as the leading error term. The approximation is second-order accurate, meaning the error scales as h². This central difference scheme is widely used in numerical analysis for solving differential equations.
finite_difference_second_derivative.history: The central difference approximation for derivatives dates back to the development of finite difference methods in the 18th century, with contributions from Taylor, Euler, and later refinements by Runge and others in the 19th century. It became standard with the advent of numerical computing.
finite_difference_second_derivative.applicability: Applies to sufficiently smooth functions (at least twice differentiable) with small step size h. Breaks down for functions with discontinuities or sharp features where h is not small enough to resolve them. Also fails for very small h due to floating-point round-off errors, and for functions with high-frequency oscillations where the sampling theorem is violated.

operators.m: flips a matrix or vector over its diagonal

quadratic_form.description: This formula defines a quadratic form, a polynomial function of degree two in the components of the vector x. It consists of a quadratic term x^T Q x, a linear term b^T x, and a constant c. The matrix Q encodes the quadratic coefficients, and its symmetry properties determine the form's behavior (e.g., positive definiteness implies convexity). This representation is fundamental in optimization, statistics, and physics for describing energy surfaces or potentials.
quadratic_form.history: Quadratic forms have been studied since the 19th century, with significant contributions by mathematicians like Gauss and Sylvester. The matrix-vector notation became standard in the 20th century with the development of linear algebra.
quadratic_form.applicability: This formula applies to any system where the function is a polynomial of degree two, such as harmonic potentials in mechanics or cost functions in optimization. It breaks down when the function has higher-order terms or is non-polynomial, requiring more general representations.

penalized_optimization.description: This formula represents a penalized optimization objective, combining a primary objective g(x) with a penalty term λ h(x) that enforces constraints or regularization. The parameter λ controls the trade-off between minimizing g and satisfying the penalty. This formulation is widely used in constrained optimization, where h(x) measures constraint violation, and in regularization, where h(x) promotes desirable properties like sparsity.
penalized_optimization.history: Penalty methods date back to the 1940s with work by Courant and others. The modern formulation with a tunable λ parameter became standard in optimization literature during the 1960s and 1970s.
penalized_optimization.applicability: This applies to optimization problems where constraints can be expressed as penalty functions, including linear and nonlinear programming. It breaks down when the penalty function is non-smooth or when λ must be infinite to enforce hard constraints, requiring exact penalty methods or augmented Lagrangian approaches.

operators.m: returns the magnitude of a real number

linear_dispersion_relation.description: This dispersion relation states that the angular frequency ω of a wave is directly proportional to the magnitude of its wave number k, with the proportionality constant c being the wave speed. It describes non-dispersive propagation, meaning all frequency components travel at the same speed, preserving the wave's shape. This relation holds for massless excitations like electromagnetic waves in vacuum or sound waves in a homogeneous medium.
linear_dispersion_relation.history: The linear dispersion relation for light was established by Maxwell's equations in the 1860s, predicting c as the speed of light. For sound, it was derived from the wave equation in the 18th century by d'Alembert and others.
linear_dispersion_relation.applicability: This applies to wave propagation in homogeneous, isotropic, non-dispersive media, such as electromagnetic waves in vacuum or acoustic waves in ideal gases. It breaks down in dispersive media where ω is a nonlinear function of k, in anisotropic materials, or when the medium has boundaries or inhomogeneities that cause mode coupling.

variables.m: de Broglie wavelength of the particle

constants.m: Planck constant, the quantum of action

de_broglie_wavelength.description: The de Broglie wavelength relates a particle's momentum to a wave-like wavelength, establishing wave-particle duality. It states that every massive particle has an associated wavelength inversely proportional to its momentum. This relation is fundamental to quantum mechanics, underpinning phenomena like electron diffraction. It holds for any particle, from electrons to macroscopic objects, though the wavelength becomes negligible for large masses.
de_broglie_wavelength.history: Proposed by Louis de Broglie in 1924 in his doctoral thesis, extending the wave-particle duality of light to matter. It was later confirmed experimentally by Davisson and Germer in 1927 through electron diffraction.
de_broglie_wavelength.applicability: Applies to all matter, but is practically significant only for microscopic particles where the wavelength is comparable to experimental scales. It breaks down in the relativistic regime where momentum must be replaced by the relativistic expression, and for massless particles like photons, where momentum is defined via energy. It is a non-relativistic approximation valid when the particle's speed is much less than the speed of light.

operators.m: computes the gradient of the error with respect to the parameter

gradient_descent_update.description: This is the gradient descent update rule used in optimization, particularly in machine learning. It adjusts a parameter by subtracting the product of a learning rate and the gradient of the error function with respect to that parameter. The update moves the parameter in the direction of steepest descent of the error surface. This iterative process aims to minimize the error function. The learning rate controls the size of each step.
gradient_descent_update.history: The method originates from Cauchy's work in 1847 on gradient-based optimization. Its modern form in machine learning was popularized in the 1950s-60s with the advent of neural networks, notably by Rosenblatt and later by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams in 1986 for backpropagation.
gradient_descent_update.applicability: Applies to differentiable error functions and is widely used in training neural networks. It assumes the error surface is smooth enough for local gradient information to be useful. It breaks down for non-differentiable functions, highly non-convex landscapes where it may get stuck in local minima, and when the learning rate is too large causing divergence. Variants like stochastic gradient descent relax the requirement of using the full dataset for each gradient computation.

variables.m: distance between the centers of mass
unit vector pointing from one mass to the other

constants.m: Newtonian gravitational constant, fundamental constant of gravitation

newtons_law_of_universal_gravitation.description: Newton's law of universal gravitation states that every point mass attracts every other point mass with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The force acts along the line joining the two masses. This law successfully describes planetary motion and terrestrial gravity. It is a central force law, meaning the force is directed along the line connecting the centers.
newtons_law_of_universal_gravitation.history: Formulated by Isaac Newton in 1687 in his 'Principia', synthesizing earlier work by Kepler and Galileo. It was the first quantitative theory of gravity, unifying celestial and terrestrial mechanics.
newtons_law_of_universal_gravitation.applicability: Applies to point masses and spherically symmetric mass distributions (by the shell theorem). It is valid for non-relativistic, weak gravitational fields. It breaks down in strong gravitational fields near massive objects like black holes and neutron stars, where general relativity is required. It also fails for very small distances where quantum effects become important, requiring a theory of quantum gravity. It assumes instantaneous action at a distance, which is incompatible with special relativity.

variables.m: Power spectral density as a function of frequency

one_over_f_noise.description: This formula states that the power spectral density of a signal or noise process scales as an inverse power of frequency, with exponent β typically close to 1. It implies that lower frequencies carry more power, leading to long-range correlations in time. The proportionality constant is system-specific and not universal. This behavior is observed in diverse systems, from electronic devices to natural phenomena like river flows and biological signals.
one_over_f_noise.history: The term '1/f noise' was coined in the mid-20th century, with early observations in vacuum tubes by Johnson in 1925 and later in semiconductors. The ubiquity of the phenomenon was recognized by the 1970s, but a single universal mechanism remains elusive.
one_over_f_noise.applicability: This scaling applies to stationary stochastic processes over a limited frequency range, typically many decades but not down to zero frequency. It breaks down at very low frequencies where the spectrum must flatten to have finite total power, and at high frequencies where other noise sources (e.g., white noise) dominate. The exponent β varies by system, so the formula is not universal in its exact form.

variables.m: Infinitesimal heat added to the system
Infinitesimal work done by the system

operators.m: Exact differential of a state function
Inexact differential for path-dependent quantities

first_law_thermodynamics.description: The first law of thermodynamics expresses energy conservation for a thermodynamic system. It states that the change in internal energy equals the heat added to the system minus the work done by the system. The use of δ for heat and work indicates they are path-dependent, while dU is an exact differential of the state function U. This law holds for any process, reversible or irreversible, as long as the system is closed (no mass transfer).
first_law_thermodynamics.history: The first law was formulated in the mid-19th century, with contributions from Mayer, Joule, and Helmholtz. It emerged from experiments on mechanical equivalence of heat and was formalized by Clausius in 1850.
first_law_thermodynamics.applicability: This law applies to closed systems where only energy transfer occurs, not mass. It breaks down for open systems where matter crosses boundaries, requiring additional terms for chemical potential. It also assumes a well-defined internal energy, which holds for equilibrium states but may be ambiguous for far-from-equilibrium processes.

carnot_efficiency.description: The Carnot efficiency gives the maximum possible efficiency of a heat engine operating between two thermal reservoirs at temperatures T_h and T_c. It is derived from the second law of thermodynamics and assumes a reversible cycle. The efficiency approaches 1 as T_c approaches zero or T_h approaches infinity, but never reaches 1 for finite temperatures. Real engines have lower efficiency due to irreversibilities.
carnot_efficiency.history: Sadi Carnot introduced this concept in 1824 in his work 'Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire'. The formula was later refined by Clausius and Kelvin in the 1850s as the second law was formalized.
carnot_efficiency.applicability: This formula applies to any heat engine operating between two reservoirs, assuming reversible processes and no other energy transfers. It breaks down for engines with more than two reservoirs, for non-thermal energy sources (e.g., chemical or nuclear), and for systems where quantum effects dominate. It also assumes the reservoirs are infinite and at constant temperature.

operators.m: Derivative with respect to radial coordinate

tolman_oppenheimer_volkoff.description: The Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) equation governs the hydrostatic equilibrium of a spherically symmetric, static, relativistic star. It generalizes the Newtonian equation of hydrostatic equilibrium by including pressure contributions to the gravitational mass-energy and the curvature of spacetime. The equation arises from the Einstein field equations for a perfect fluid with a given equation of state relating pressure and energy density. It determines the pressure gradient needed to counteract gravitational collapse.
tolman_oppenheimer_volkoff.history: Derived independently by Richard C. Tolman (1939) and J. Robert Oppenheimer and George Volkoff (1939) in the context of neutron star structure. It remains the standard equation for relativistic stellar structure.
tolman_oppenheimer_volkoff.applicability: Valid for static, spherically symmetric, non-rotating stars in general relativity. Assumes a perfect fluid with no shear stresses or heat flow. Breaks down for rapidly rotating stars (requires Hartle-Thorne formalism), anisotropic pressures, or when magnetic fields are significant. Also fails near the formation of an event horizon where the equation becomes singular.

operators.m: Quantum mechanical inner product
Sum over states

quantum_probability_amplitude.description: This formula expresses the probability amplitude for a quantum system in thermal equilibrium to be found in a particular state χ_k. It sums over all energy eigenstates n, weighted by the Boltzmann factor P_n, the overlap between the target state and the energy eigenstate. The result gives the amplitude whose squared modulus yields the probability of observing the system in state χ_k. It connects statistical mechanics with quantum measurement theory.
quantum_probability_amplitude.history: The formula emerges from the standard framework of quantum statistical mechanics developed in the 1920s-1930s by von Neumann, Dirac, and others. It is a direct application of the density matrix formalism to probability amplitudes.
quantum_probability_amplitude.applicability: Valid for systems in thermal equilibrium described by a canonical ensemble. Assumes the Boltzmann weights P_n are properly normalized and that the states form a complete basis. Breaks down for non-equilibrium systems, open quantum systems with decoherence, or when the Hilbert space is truncated inappropriately.

variables.m: Lensed gravitational wave signal in frequency domain
Time delay of image j relative to source

operators.m: Sum over lensed images
Complex exponential encoding phase shifts

gravitational_lensing_signal.description: This formula describes how gravitational waves are modified by gravitational lensing from a massive object. Each lensed image j contributes to the observed signal with a magnification factor μ_j, a time delay Δt_j, and a phase shift determined by the Morse index n_j. The total lensed signal is the coherent sum of these contributions. This is the gravitational wave analogue of the lensing of electromagnetic waves, but with additional phase effects due to wave optics.
gravitational_lensing_signal.history: The formalism was developed in the 2000s-2010s as gravitational wave astronomy emerged. Key contributions came from Takahashi and Nakamura (2003) and later works by Dai, Venumadhav, and others (2017-2018) who applied it to LIGO/Virgo sources.
gravitational_lensing_signal.applicability: Valid in the geometric optics limit where the gravitational wavelength is much smaller than the lens scale. Assumes a static, thin lens and weak gravitational fields. Breaks down for very long wavelengths (wave optics regime), strongly nonlinear lenses, or when the source is not point-like. Also fails for overlapping signals or when the lens itself is moving significantly during the observation.

constants.m: Universal constant of gravitation
Speed of light in vacuum

einstein_field_equations.description: The Einstein field equations relate the geometry of spacetime, encoded in the Einstein tensor, to the local energy-momentum distribution. They are the core of general relativity, stating that matter and energy curve spacetime, and this curvature dictates how matter moves. The equations are a set of ten coupled nonlinear partial differential equations. They reduce to Newtonian gravity in the weak-field, slow-motion limit.
einstein_field_equations.history: Albert Einstein derived the field equations in November 1915, after several years of work and with input from Marcel Grossmann and David Hilbert. The final form was presented to the Prussian Academy of Sciences on November 25, 1915.
einstein_field_equations.applicability: The equations apply to macroscopic scales where quantum effects of gravity are negligible, and spacetime is treated as a smooth four-dimensional manifold. They break down at singularities (e.g., black hole centers, the Big Bang) where quantum gravity is expected to be necessary. They also fail to describe the strong-field regime where quantum effects become significant, and are not applicable to systems where the gravitational field is extremely weak and velocities are low without reducing to Newtonian gravity.

variables.m: Conductance when magnetic layers are parallel
Conductance when magnetic layers are antiparallel

tunneling_magnetoresistance.description: Tunneling magnetoresistance quantifies the relative change in electrical resistance when the magnetization directions of two ferromagnetic layers separated by a thin insulating barrier switch from parallel to antiparallel. The effect arises from spin-dependent tunneling probabilities, where the density of states at the Fermi level differs for majority and minority spins. A higher TMR ratio indicates a larger difference in conductance between the two magnetic configurations, which is exploited in magnetic tunnel junctions for read heads and magnetic random-access memory.
tunneling_magnetoresistance.history: The effect was first observed by Michel Jullière in 1975 in Fe/Ge/Co junctions at low temperatures, but the term and practical significance grew after the discovery of large room-temperature TMR in the 1990s, particularly with the work of Moodera and Miyazaki.
tunneling_magnetoresistance.applicability: The formula applies to magnetic tunnel junctions with a thin insulating barrier where coherent tunneling dominates. It assumes the two magnetic layers are identical and the barrier is uniform. It breaks down for very thick barriers where direct tunneling is negligible, or at high bias voltages where inelastic tunneling and other effects become significant. It also assumes the magnetization directions are strictly parallel or antiparallel, not at intermediate angles.

variables.m: Electrical conductance of a mesoscopic conductor
Transmission probability for an electron at energy E

operators.m: Sum over all transmission channels or energy levels

constants.m: Magnitude of the charge of an electron
Planck constant, fundamental quantum of action

landauer_formula.description: The Landauer formula expresses the electrical conductance of a mesoscopic conductor in terms of the quantum mechanical transmission probabilities of its conduction channels. It shows that conductance is quantized in units of e²/h, the conductance quantum, multiplied by the total transmission. The formula connects the macroscopic transport property to microscopic quantum scattering, and is fundamental to understanding quantum transport in nanostructures. It assumes coherent transport, where electrons traverse the conductor without phase-breaking scattering.
landauer_formula.history: Rolf Landauer formulated this relation in 1957, and it was later extended by Markus Büttiker in the 1980s to multi-terminal systems. The formula became central to mesoscopic physics after the discovery of quantized conductance in quantum point contacts in 1988.
landauer_formula.applicability: The formula applies to mesoscopic conductors where electron transport is coherent, meaning the phase of the electron wavefunction is preserved across the device. It is valid at low temperatures and for short conductors where inelastic scattering is negligible. It breaks down for macroscopic conductors where diffusive transport and phase-breaking processes dominate, and for systems with strong electron-electron interactions where the single-particle picture fails. It also assumes the contacts are ideal and the conductor is connected to reservoirs in thermal equilibrium.

operators.m: Derivative with respect to cosmic time

slow_roll_parameter.description: This formula defines the first slow-roll parameter as the negative logarithmic rate of change of the Hubble parameter. During inflation, this parameter is much less than unity, indicating that the Hubble parameter changes slowly compared to the expansion rate. It quantifies the deviation from exact de Sitter expansion, where H is constant. The condition ε << 1 is necessary for sustained accelerated expansion.
slow_roll_parameter.history: The slow-roll formalism was developed in the early 1980s by theorists including Alan Guth, Andrei Linde, and others, building on the inflationary paradigm. The specific parameterization in terms of H and its derivative became standard in the late 1980s with the work of Liddle and Lyth.
slow_roll_parameter.applicability: This parameter applies to single-field slow-roll inflation models where the inflaton field evolves slowly. It breaks down in non-slow-roll scenarios such as ultra-slow-roll inflation or models with significant kinetic energy contributions. It also assumes a homogeneous and isotropic background, so it does not apply to inhomogeneous perturbations.

inflationary_spectral_indices.description: These relations connect the slow-roll parameters to observable quantities in the cosmic microwave background. The scalar spectral index n_s measures the scale dependence of the primordial curvature perturbations, with n_s = 1 corresponding to a scale-invariant spectrum. The tensor-to-scalar ratio r quantifies the relative amplitude of gravitational waves to density perturbations. Both are derived from the power spectra of perturbations generated during inflation.
inflationary_spectral_indices.history: These relations were derived in the late 1980s and early 1990s by Mukhanov, Chibisov, and others, building on the theory of quantum fluctuations during inflation. The specific slow-roll expressions became standard with the work of Liddle and Lyth in the early 1990s.
inflationary_spectral_indices.applicability: These formulas apply to single-field slow-roll inflation models with canonical kinetic terms. They break down in multi-field models, non-canonical kinetic terms (e.g., DBI inflation), or when slow-roll conditions are violated. They also assume the perturbations are generated from vacuum fluctuations and that the modes are well outside the horizon at the time of observation.

variables.m: Transition rate from initial state i to final state f
Density of final states at energy E_f

operators.m: Matrix element of the perturbation between initial and final states

constants.m: Reduced Planck constant, relating energy to angular frequency

fermis_golden_rule.description: Fermi's golden rule gives the transition rate from an initial quantum state to a continuum of final states under a weak perturbation. The rate is proportional to the square of the matrix element of the perturbation and the density of final states. It is derived from first-order time-dependent perturbation theory, assuming the perturbation is turned on adiabatically. The factor 2π/ħ ensures the correct normalization for the transition probability per unit time.
fermis_golden_rule.history: The rule was developed by Paul Dirac in the 1920s and later formalized by Enrico Fermi, who popularized it in his 1950 book 'Nuclear Physics'. It is called 'golden' because of its wide applicability in quantum mechanics.
fermis_golden_rule.applicability: This rule applies to weak perturbations where first-order perturbation theory is valid, and the final states form a continuum. It breaks down for strong perturbations, when higher-order terms become significant, or when the density of states varies rapidly over the energy range. It also assumes the perturbation is time-independent or varies slowly compared to the transition time.

variables.m: Dispersion measure from Milky Way interstellar medium
Dispersion measure from Milky Way halo

dispersion_measure_sum.description: The observed dispersion measure of a fast radio burst or pulsar is the integral of free electron density along the line of sight. This formula decomposes that total into additive contributions from distinct regions: the Milky Way's interstellar medium, the Milky Way's halo, the intergalactic medium (large-scale structure), and the host galaxy. The host contribution is divided by (1+z) because the observed frequency is redshifted, which reduces the measured dispersion measure for a given rest-frame electron column. This decomposition is essential for isolating the cosmological signal from local foregrounds.
dispersion_measure_sum.history: The concept of dispersion measure dates to early pulsar astronomy in the 1960s, with the decomposition into separate components becoming standard practice in fast radio burst studies in the 2010s. The formula's modern form emerged from community efforts to standardize DM accounting, particularly in the context of FRB cosmology.
dispersion_measure_sum.applicability: This formula applies to extragalactic radio transients like fast radio bursts and pulsars in other galaxies, where the line of sight passes through distinct electron reservoirs. It assumes that the contributions are additive, which holds when the electron density fluctuations in each region are independent and the geometric path is well approximated. It breaks down for sources within the Milky Way where the host and MW ISM terms overlap, or when the intergalactic medium is highly clumpy and the mean DM is not representative. The (1+z) scaling assumes the host contribution is measured in the rest frame and that the source is at cosmological distance.

variables.m: Angular power spectrum at multipole ell
Window function (selection function) at redshift z
Three-dimensional power spectrum at wavenumber k and redshift z

operators.m: Sum over all redshifts along the line of sight

constants.m: Fundamental constant relating distance and time in relativity

limber_approximation.description: The Limber approximation simplifies the computation of angular power spectra by relating them to the three-dimensional matter power spectrum through a projection integral. It replaces the full spherical harmonic transform with a local mapping between multipole ell and wavenumber k = (ell+1/2)/chi(z), assuming that the dominant contribution comes from modes perpendicular to the line of sight. The factor H(z)/(c chi^2) accounts for the volume element and the geometry of the projection. This approximation is widely used in cosmology to compute CMB lensing, galaxy clustering, and weak lensing spectra.
limber_approximation.history: The approximation was introduced by D. Nelson Limber in 1953 in the context of galaxy clustering. It was later generalized and applied to cosmological power spectra by Kaiser (1992) and others, becoming a standard tool in large-scale structure analyses.
limber_approximation.applicability: The Limber approximation is valid when the window function W(z) is broad compared to the wavelength of the fluctuations, i.e., when the radial extent of the selection function is much larger than the correlation length. It breaks down for low multipoles (ell < 10) where the flat-sky approximation fails and for very narrow window functions, such as those from spectroscopic surveys with thin redshift slices. It also assumes linear or mildly nonlinear clustering and a flat or nearly flat universe, though corrections exist for curved geometries.

variables.m: Semi-major axis of the binary orbit
Reduced mass of the binary system
Total mass of the binary system

constants.m: Fundamental constant relating distance and time in relativity
Constant determining the strength of gravitational force

gravitational_wave_coalescence_time.description: This formula gives the time for a binary system of two point masses to merge due to the emission of gravitational waves, as predicted by general relativity. The coalescence time scales as the fourth power of the orbital separation and inversely with the product of the reduced mass and the square of the total mass. The factor (1-e^2)^{7/2} accounts for the enhancement of gravitational wave emission in eccentric orbits, which shortens the coalescence time. This result is derived from the quadrupole formula for gravitational radiation, assuming a circular orbit in the leading-order approximation.
gravitational_wave_coalescence_time.history: The formula was derived by Peters and Mathews in 1963, building on earlier work by Einstein and others on gravitational radiation. Peters (1964) extended it to eccentric orbits, providing the full expression including the eccentricity dependence.
gravitational_wave_coalescence_time.applicability: This formula applies to compact binaries (e.g., neutron star or black hole binaries) in the weak-field, slow-motion regime, where the orbital velocity is much less than the speed of light and the gravitational field is weak. It assumes the orbit evolves quasi-statically through a sequence of Keplerian orbits, which holds for most of the inspiral phase. It breaks down in the final stages of merger when the orbital velocity approaches the speed of light and strong-field effects become important; then numerical relativity is required. It also neglects the effect of tidal deformation and spin-orbit coupling, which can be significant for neutron star binaries.

variables.m: distance of closest approach in absence of gravity
speed of the test particle at infinity

operators.m: takes the square root of the argument

constants.m: Universal constant of gravitation

gravitational_deflection.description: This formula gives the impact parameter b for a test particle (e.g., a photon or massive particle) undergoing gravitational scattering by a point mass M, in the weak-field, small-deflection approximation. It relates the unperturbed closest approach distance q to the actual impact parameter, incorporating the gravitational potential energy relative to the kinetic energy at infinity. The expression arises from solving the geodesic equation in a Schwarzschild metric to first order in GM/(q v_infinity^2). It shows that the impact parameter is slightly larger than q due to gravitational attraction.
gravitational_deflection.history: This form is derived from the classical Rutherford-like scattering analogy applied to gravity, developed in the early 20th century. It is a standard result in celestial mechanics and general relativity, often attributed to the work of Einstein and others in the context of gravitational deflection.
gravitational_deflection.applicability: This formula applies to weak gravitational fields where GM/(q v_infinity^2) is small, and for test particles moving at non-relativistic speeds (v_infinity << c). It breaks down for strong fields (e.g., near a black hole), for relativistic speeds where the full geodesic equation is needed, and when the deflection angle is large. It also assumes a point mass and ignores the finite size of the deflecting body.

variables.m: distance of closest approach in absence of gravity
radial distance from the gravitating body
speed of the test particle at infinity

operators.m: trigonometric sine function
takes the square root of the argument

constants.m: Universal constant of gravitation

gravitational_deflection_angle.description: This formula gives the sine of the deflection angle theta for a test particle in a gravitational field, relating it to the ratio q/r and the gravitational potential energy relative to kinetic energy. It describes how the trajectory bends as the particle moves from a radial distance r to infinity, in the weak-field approximation. The expression is derived from the conservation of angular momentum and energy in a Schwarzschild metric, keeping terms to first order in GM/(r v_infinity^2). It shows that the deflection increases as the particle approaches the mass (smaller r) and as the mass increases.
gravitational_deflection_angle.history: This formula is part of the classical treatment of gravitational scattering, developed in the context of general relativity in the early 20th century. It is a standard result in textbooks on general relativity and celestial mechanics, often used to compute the bending of light or massive particles.
gravitational_deflection_angle.applicability: This formula applies to weak gravitational fields (GM/(r v_infinity^2) << 1) and for non-relativistic test particles (v_infinity << c). It breaks down for strong fields, relativistic speeds, and when the deflection angle is large. It assumes a point mass and ignores the finite size of the deflecting body. For light (v_infinity = c), the formula must be modified to include relativistic effects.

operators.m: statistical variance of a random variable
asymptotically proportional to (up to a constant factor)
some function of the spectral dimension

variance_scaling.description: This formula states that the variance of a random variable X_n scales asymptotically as some function f of the spectral dimension d_s. The spectral dimension characterizes the effective dimensionality of a space or network as probed by a random walk. This scaling law is common in the study of diffusion on fractals, disordered media, and complex networks, where the variance of a quantity (e.g., displacement) grows with a power of the number of steps n, with the exponent determined by d_s. The exact form of f depends on the specific system and the quantity being measured.
variance_scaling.history: This scaling relation emerged from the theory of random walks on fractals and disordered systems, developed in the 1980s by researchers such as Alexander and Orbach, and later extended to complex networks. It is a phenomenological law that captures the universal behavior of diffusion in non-integer dimensions.
variance_scaling.applicability: This formula applies to systems where a random walk or diffusion process occurs on a structure with a well-defined spectral dimension, such as fractals, percolation clusters, and certain networks. It holds in the asymptotic limit of large n (many steps) and assumes the process is stationary and ergodic. It breaks down for finite n, for systems without a clear spectral dimension, or when the random walk is not Markovian. The specific form of f must be determined for each system, and the scaling may fail in the presence of strong correlations or traps.

variables.m: Coefficient function for each Γ_α term
Matrix representing hopping and on-site terms

operators.m: Sum over all relevant terms α

tight_binding_hamiltonian.description: The tight-binding Hamiltonian describes electrons in a periodic lattice by expanding the Hamiltonian in a basis of localized atomic orbitals. The coefficients c_α(k) encode the energy dispersion, while the matrices Γ_α represent the hopping amplitudes and on-site energies in this basis. This form is useful for studying band structure and topological properties of crystals.
tight_binding_hamiltonian.history: The tight-binding method was developed in the early days of quantum mechanics, with contributions from Bloch (1928) and later systematized by Slater and Koster (1954) for practical calculations.
tight_binding_hamiltonian.applicability: This model applies to systems where electrons are tightly bound to atoms, such as transition metals, semiconductors, and many organic crystals. It breaks down for nearly free electron systems, where the plane-wave basis is more appropriate, and for strongly correlated systems where interactions beyond single-particle approximation are significant.

operators.m: Derivative with respect to cosmic time

energy_conservation_interacting_fluids.description: These equations describe the energy conservation for two interacting fluids in an expanding universe. Each fluid's energy density changes due to cosmic expansion (the Hubble drag term) and due to energy exchange Q between them. The total energy density ρ_1 + ρ_2 is conserved when the two equations are summed, as the exchange terms cancel.
energy_conservation_interacting_fluids.history: This formalism is standard in cosmology, developed in the context of interacting dark energy and dark matter models. It has been used extensively since the late 1990s to study energy transfer between cosmic components.
energy_conservation_interacting_fluids.applicability: This applies to homogeneous and isotropic cosmologies (Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker metric) where fluids are perfect and minimally coupled. It breaks down for anisotropic or inhomogeneous models, and when the fluids have non-trivial bulk viscosity or shear stresses.

operators.m: Sum over all components i
Natural logarithm

constants.m: Universal gas constant relating energy scale to temperature

entropy_of_mixing.description: This formula gives the entropy increase when ideal gases are mixed at constant temperature and pressure. The entropy of mixing arises because each component expands into the total volume, increasing the number of accessible microstates. It is always positive since mole fractions are between 0 and 1, making the logarithm negative and the overall expression positive.
entropy_of_mixing.history: The entropy of mixing formula was derived by Gibbs in the 1870s as part of his work on the thermodynamics of mixtures. It is a cornerstone of statistical mechanics and solution theory.
entropy_of_mixing.applicability: This applies to ideal solutions and ideal gas mixtures where interactions between different components are negligible. It breaks down for real solutions with strong intermolecular forces, where activity coefficients must be introduced, and for mixtures of isotopes where quantum effects can alter the entropy.

variables.m: Hull enthalpy, energy above convex hull
Convex hull energy at the composition

hull_enthalpy_stability.description: This criterion defines the thermodynamic stability of a compound relative to competing phases. The hull enthalpy is the difference between the compound's formation enthalpy and the convex hull energy at the same composition. A positive value means the compound lies above the convex hull and is thermodynamically unstable, tending to decompose into more stable phases. A negative or zero value indicates stability or metastability with respect to decomposition.
hull_enthalpy_stability.history: The convex hull construction is a standard tool in computational thermodynamics, developed through the 20th century for phase diagram analysis. Its systematic application to materials stability screening became widespread with high-throughput density functional theory in the 2000s.
hull_enthalpy_stability.applicability: This criterion applies to solid compounds at zero temperature and pressure, as typically computed by DFT. It breaks down at finite temperatures where vibrational and configurational entropy contributions become significant, and for systems where kinetic barriers prevent decomposition despite thermodynamic instability.

axion_photon_coupling_rotation.description: This formula describes the rotation of photon polarization due to a spatially varying axion field. The rotation angle is proportional to the axion-photon coupling and the field difference along the photon path. This effect arises from the axion-photon interaction term in the Lagrangian, which mixes the two polarization states. The rotation is analogous to the Faraday effect but driven by the axion field rather than a magnetic field.
axion_photon_coupling_rotation.history: The axion-photon coupling was proposed in the late 1970s and early 1980s in the context of Peccei-Quinn symmetry breaking. The polarization rotation effect was identified as a possible observational signature by Sikivie and others in the 1980s.
axion_photon_coupling_rotation.applicability: This linearized formula applies for small rotation angles and slowly varying axion fields. It breaks down for strong couplings or large field gradients where higher-order terms become important, and for photon energies near the axion mass where resonant effects occur.

axion_oscillation_amplitude.description: This formula gives the amplitude of polarization oscillations induced by axion dark matter. The axion field oscillates with frequency set by its mass, and through the axion-photon coupling this produces a periodic rotation of photon polarization. The amplitude depends on the coupling strength and the square root of the local dark matter density divided by the axion mass. This effect provides a potential direct detection strategy for axion dark matter.
axion_oscillation_amplitude.history: This expression emerged from studies of axion dark matter detection in the 1980s and 1990s, particularly in the context of laser interferometry experiments. It was refined as part of the theoretical framework for axion haloscopes and helioscopes.
axion_oscillation_amplitude.applicability: This formula assumes a homogeneous, coherently oscillating axion field, valid for the standard cold dark matter scenario. It breaks down for axion masses where the coherence time is shorter than the measurement duration, and for non-standard dark matter distributions with significant small-scale structure.

variables.m: Angular radius of the Einstein ring
Angular diameter distance between lens and source
Angular diameter distance from observer to lens
Angular diameter distance from observer to source

operators.m: Takes the square root of the argument

einstein_ring_radius.description: This formula gives the angular radius of the Einstein ring, which is the apparent circular image of a background source formed when a point mass acts as a gravitational lens. It arises from the bending of light in a Schwarzschild spacetime, assuming a thin lens and small angles. The radius depends on the lens mass and the relative distances between observer, lens, and source. It is a key quantity in gravitational lensing, determining the scale of image separation and magnification.
einstein_ring_radius.history: The concept was first derived by Albert Einstein in 1936 in a brief paper, though he considered the effect unlikely to be observed. The formula was later generalized and applied in modern lensing theory, particularly by Jürgen Ehlers and others in the 1960s–70s.
einstein_ring_radius.applicability: This formula applies to a point-mass lens in a static, spherically symmetric spacetime, under the thin-lens approximation and small-angle limit. It breaks down for extended mass distributions, where the lensing is described by the full lens equation, and for strong fields where higher-order corrections are needed. It also assumes a Euclidean background geometry for the distances, which is valid only in a flat universe or for local measurements.

variables.m: Angular radius of the Einstein ring
Relative proper motion between lens and source

einstein_timescale.description: This formula defines the Einstein crossing time as the ratio of the Einstein angular radius to the relative proper motion between the lens and the source. It represents the characteristic timescale over which a microlensing event evolves, as the source moves behind the lens. The timescale is a crucial observable in microlensing surveys, allowing estimation of the lens mass and distance when combined with other constraints.
einstein_timescale.history: The concept was introduced in the context of gravitational microlensing in the 1980s, particularly by Bohdan Paczyński in his 1986 paper proposing the search for dark matter via microlensing. The formula itself is a straightforward definition from kinematics.
einstein_timescale.applicability: This formula applies to microlensing events where the relative motion is uniform and the lens is a point mass. It assumes a constant proper motion and no parallax effects. It breaks down for events with significant acceleration, such as binary lenses or when the source is extended, and for high-precision measurements where finite-source effects or orbital motion of the Earth must be considered.

variables.m: Mass ratio of the binary system

mass_ratio.description: This formula defines the mass ratio of a binary system as the quotient of the secondary mass to the primary mass. It is a dimensionless parameter that characterizes the mass distribution in a binary, often used in studies of stellar evolution, orbital dynamics, and gravitational wave sources. The convention assumes m_1 ≥ m_2, so q ≤ 1, but the definition can be inverted depending on context.
mass_ratio.history: The concept of mass ratio has been used in celestial mechanics since the early studies of binary stars in the 19th century. Its formal definition as a ratio is standard in astronomy and has been adopted in modern astrophysics without a single attributed origin.
mass_ratio.applicability: This definition applies to any binary system, whether stellar, planetary, or black hole binaries, as long as masses are well-defined. It is universally applicable but becomes less meaningful for systems with significant mass exchange or where the components are not distinct. In relativistic contexts, the mass ratio is still used, but care is needed when defining masses in strong gravity.

constants.m: Universal constant of gravitation
Planck constant divided by 2π

quantum_jeans_scale.description: This formula defines the wavenumber at which the quantum pressure gradient (arising from the Heisenberg uncertainty principle) exactly balances the gravitational attraction in a uniform medium of bosonic particles of mass m and density ρ. For perturbations with wavenumber larger than k_qJ, quantum pressure prevents gravitational collapse, while for smaller wavenumbers gravity dominates. It is the quantum analogue of the classical Jeans scale, replacing thermal pressure with quantum pressure.
quantum_jeans_scale.history: The concept emerged from studies of Bose-Einstein condensates in astrophysical contexts, particularly in the 1990s–2000s with the development of fuzzy dark matter models. It is not attributed to a single author but grew from the application of quantum hydrodynamics to cosmological structure formation.
quantum_jeans_scale.applicability: This formula applies to a non-relativistic, zero-temperature Bose gas where quantum pressure is the sole support mechanism against gravity. It breaks down when the system is relativistic, when interactions between particles are significant (requiring a modified equation of state), or when the density varies on scales comparable to the quantum wavelength. It also assumes a homogeneous background density.

constants.m: Universal constant of gravitation
